passage: Beta, you want to know about best friends? When I was ten, in our lane in Lucknow, Naveen was mine. Only mine. People called me Farhan the shadow. We shared one bicycle, one tiffin and every secret. I told him I was scared of the dark and still slept holding Ammi's dupatta. He swore on his cricket bat he'd never tell. Two weeks later, in front of the whole class, he said it out loud, and everyone laughed. I went home and wouldn't eat. It felt as if the floor had gone. For a month I sat alone. Then Naveen came to our gate, red in the face, and said sorry. I forgave him slowly. Your Dadi says I still pick friends carefully. But I still pick them.

qa.q: What secret did Farhan tell Naveen?
qa.a: That Farhan was scared of the dark and still slept holding Ammi's dupatta.

qa.q: How did Farhan feel after Naveen told the class?
qa.a: Farhan felt devastated and betrayed, refused to eat at home and felt as if the floor had gone.

qa.q: When Naveen came to the gate, what choice did Farhan face, and what came of it?
qa.a: Farhan could stay shut off or forgive slowly. Forgiving slowly saved the friendship and led to careful trust instead of no trust.

qa.q: Why might Naveen have come to the gate red in the face?
qa.a: He probably felt ashamed of breaking his promise and missed his best friend after a month apart.

grounding: An elder recalls a childhood best friend who shared every secret and then betrayed one, leaving deep hurt that slowly healed.

passage: Rain hammered the school bus roof, and the only empty seat was next to Shreya. Manjula stood in the aisle, dripping, clutching her bag. That morning Ruchika had whispered, "Is it true you're moving to a one-room flat?" Only one person knew that. Manjula had told Shreya under the slide last week, pinkie-swear, best friends forever. "Sit down, child, the bus is moving," the conductor called. Manjula sat, pressed against the window. Shreya leaned over. "Manju, I only told Ruchika because she asked why you looked sad..." Manjula turned to the fogged glass. Her throat hurt. She had never told anyone a real secret before Shreya, and now she didn't know if she ever would again.

qa.q: Where had Manjula told Shreya her secret?
qa.a: Under the slide last week, with a pinkie-swear.

qa.q: What does Manjula turning to the fogged glass suggest she feels?
qa.a: She feels deeply hurt and betrayed and can't face Shreya yet; her sore throat shows she is close to tears.

qa.q: What could Manjula do once she's ready, instead of deciding never to share again?
qa.a: She could tell Shreya how much it hurt and hear the explanation, then decide slowly how far to trust again rather than shutting everyone out.

qa.q: How might Shreya be feeling as Manjula turns away?
qa.a: Shreya may feel guilty and panicky, trying to explain and afraid of losing a best friend 😔

grounding: A child whose one best friend passes on her secret feels crushed, showing how much the close friendship meant.

passage: Every evening in their Pune colony, Ramesh and Yamini climbed onto the water-tank ledge, the one place grown-ups never checked. There Ramesh told her things he told nobody: that he was scared of the new maths teacher, that he had cried at the end of a film. Yamini shared her own secrets, and together they drew a map of the colony with their hideouts marked in red. On Monday the science-fair pairs went up on the board. They had promised to be partners. But Yamini's name was next to Pallavi's. She had signed up on Friday without a word. Ramesh walked home the long way, kicking a stone. At dinner he pushed his dal around, and when his mother asked, he said, "Nothing," and went to bed early.

qa.q: Where did Ramesh and Yamini go every evening?
qa.a: They climbed onto the water-tank ledge in their Pune colony.

qa.q: What does Ramesh saying "Nothing" and going to bed early suggest he is feeling?
qa.a: He feels betrayed and too hurt to talk; the broken promise from his closest friend has knocked him flat.

qa.q: What could Ramesh try the next day instead of avoiding Yamini?
qa.a: He could ask her on the ledge why she signed up without telling him and say how it felt, which gives the friendship a chance to mend.

qa.q: How might Ramesh's mother see his quiet evening?
qa.a: She can tell from the pushed-around dal that something is wrong, and may worry and want to help gently without forcing him to talk.

grounding: A child who shares secrets with one best friend is shattered when she breaks their promise, showing the risk and depth of that closeness.

passage:
"Sonali, why is your tiffin still full?"
"Not hungry, Bhaiya."
Saurabh sat on the edge of her bed. "Something happened."
"Gunjan read my poem out in class. The one about Nani. I only showed it to her. Only her." Her voice cracked. "Everyone laughed at the line about Nani's hands."
"She's your best friend."
"Is. Was. I don't know." Sonali pushed her face into the pillow. "I told her everything, Bhaiya. Everything."
"Did she say sorry?"
"She said it was a joke." A long pause. "Maybe I shouldn't tell anyone anything ever."
Saurabh was quiet for a while. "Or maybe you tell things to someone who keeps them. It hurts because you trusted her. That part isn't your fault."

qa.q: What did Gunjan read out in class?
qa.a: Gunjan read out Sonali's poem about Nani.

qa.q: What does Sonali mean when she says she told Gunjan 'everything'?
qa.a: She is devastated because she had opened up fully to one best friend, and that trust was broken in front of the whole class.

qa.q: When Sonali says she shouldn't tell anyone anything ever, what does Saurabh offer instead?
qa.a: He suggests trusting people who keep secrets rather than closing off completely, and tells her the trust itself was not her fault.

qa.q: Why might Gunjan have called it a joke?
qa.a: Gunjan may not have understood how private the poem was, or felt embarrassed and brushed it off, though that doesn't lessen Sonali's hurt.

grounding: A girl is devastated when her one best friend reads out her private poem, and her brother helps her not shut out closeness altogether.

passage:
I'm Francis, and I'm eleven now. When I was ten, Ankita was my best friend. We had a secret handshake and a den behind the water tank at the church hall. I told her my biggest secret: I still couldn't ride a bicycle without training wheels.
The next Monday the whole cycling group knew. Tony rang his bell at me all week. I felt like someone had pulled the floor away. I didn't eat lunch with Ankita for a month.
Later she said she only told one person. It still hurt. But I learned that telling a secret is like handing someone a glass. I still hand people glasses. I just watch first to see who holds them carefully.

qa.q: What secret did Francis tell Ankita?
qa.a: That Francis still couldn't ride a bicycle without training wheels.

qa.q: How did Francis feel when the cycling group found out?
qa.a: Francis felt like someone had pulled the floor away, let down by the one friend Francis trusted most. 😢

qa.q: What did Francis decide about sharing secrets after this?
qa.a: Francis still shares, but watches first to see who holds secrets carefully, instead of shutting everyone out.

qa.q: How might Ankita have felt when Francis stopped eating lunch with her?
qa.a: She might have felt guilty and lonely, perhaps not realising how much telling one person would hurt Francis.

grounding: A child looks back on sharing a biggest secret with one best friend, feeling devastated when she let it out, and learning to share more carefully rather than stop.

passage:
Monday: Behind the school water tank, Francis, ten, whispered to Jahnavi that he still couldn't swim. "Best friends keep everything," she said, hooking her little finger into his.
Thursday: On the pool trip, Jahnavi giggled to two girls, "Francis needs armbands!" The whole bench turned. Francis stared at the wet tiles, throat tight, and didn't talk to anyone on the bus. That night he told his mother he never wanted a best friend again. She sat on his bed, listened to all of it, and said being hurt meant he had really trusted someone.
The next Tuesday: Jahnavi pushed a folded note onto his desk: "Sorry. I wanted them to laugh with me." Francis read it twice, then slid it into his pencil box, not ready to smile yet.

qa.q: What secret did Francis whisper to Jahnavi?
qa.a: Francis whispered that he still couldn't swim.

qa.q: What was Francis feeling on the bus after the pool trip?
qa.a: He felt humiliated and betrayed, so hurt that he later said he never wanted a best friend again.

qa.q: How did Francis's mother support him, and why did it help?
qa.a: She listened to all of it and told him the hurt showed he had really trusted someone, which helped him see trust as worth something, not foolish.

qa.q: Why might Jahnavi have told the secret, according to her note?
qa.a: Jahnavi wrote that she wanted the other girls to laugh with her, so she seems to have traded Francis's trust for a moment of belonging.

grounding: A child shares a secret with his one best friend, is devastated when she betrays it, and begins learning what trusting a single peer costs and means.

passage: Vikas, you're sulking because Monty told your secret? Let me tell you about Harish. When I was eleven, in Nashik, Harish was my one real friend. I told him I was scared of the dark and slept holding my mother's shawl. Nobody else knew. At the Ganesh festival he told the whole gully, and for a month they called me "shawl-boy." I cried behind the water tank where no one could see. I decided I would never trust anybody again. But that winter Harish came to our door with his kite and said sorry, badly, staring at his feet. I made him wait a week. Then we flew that kite together off the roof. So your Suraj-dada learnt early that a friend who hurts you can still be worth the risk.

qa.q: What did the gully call Suraj for a month?
qa.a: They called him "shawl-boy" for a month.

qa.q: How did Suraj feel after Harish told the whole gully?
qa.a: Suraj felt devastated and ashamed, crying behind the water tank and deciding never to trust anybody again.

qa.q: Why was making Harish wait a week before flying the kite a sensible turning point in the story?
qa.a: It let Suraj take his hurt seriously while still leaving room for repair, so trust could return slowly instead of being cut off for good.

qa.q: How might Harish have felt standing at the door with his kite?
qa.a: Harish likely felt ashamed and nervous, which is why his apology came out badly while he stared at his feet.

grounding: An elder recalls choosing one best friend as a boy, sharing a secret, feeling devastated by the betrayal, and slowly learning to risk trust again.

passage: Rain drummed on the tin roof, PE was cancelled, and with the class teacher away at a meeting, Class 4B was stuck indoors with colouring sheets. Nandini sat beside Farida as always. Only Farida knew that Nandini still counted on her fingers under the desk during maths. Then, across the room, Rukhsar whispered loudly, "Farida says you're a finger-counter!" Nandini's crayon snapped. She stared at Farida, who went red and looked at the window. There was nowhere to go; the corridor was flooded. Nandini pressed her forehead to the desk so nobody would see her eyes. At home time Farida held out half her samosa without a word. Nandini didn't take it, but she didn't walk away either, and they waited for the rain side by side.

qa.q: What did only Farida know about Nandini?
qa.a: Only Farida knew that Nandini still counted on her fingers under the desk during maths.

qa.q: What does Nandini's snapped crayon and hidden face suggest she felt?
qa.a: They suggest she felt shocked, betrayed and embarrassed, trying to hide tears from the class.

qa.q: What could Farida try next, beyond offering the samosa?
qa.a: Farida could say sorry out loud and admit she told the secret, which would show Nandini she understands the hurt, not just want it to pass.

qa.q: What was it like for Farida when Nandini stared at her?
qa.a: Farida likely felt guilty and ashamed, turning red and looking away because she knew she had broken her best friend's trust.

grounding: A child's secret shared with her best friend is betrayed, leaving her devastated, while the friendship stays uncertainly open.

passage:
Avni and Keerthana had been best friends since Class 2 in their Hyderabad school. They sat together, swapped lunch and had a secret code for "boring class": two taps on the desk.
In Class 5, Avni told Keerthana her biggest secret: she was scared of the dark and still slept with a night lamp.
A week later, at recess, some girls giggled. "Avni needs a night lamp!"
Avni froze. Only Keerthana knew. She looked at her friend, and Keerthana went red and looked away.
Avni walked home alone, crying so hard she couldn't see the road properly. At home she told her mother she was never telling anyone anything again.
Her mother held her. "It hurts because you trusted her. That's a good thing, even when it goes wrong."

qa.q: What was Avni's secret?
qa.a: She was scared of the dark and still slept with a night lamp.

qa.q: How did Avni feel when she realised Keerthana had told her secret?
qa.a: She felt devastated and betrayed, crying so hard she couldn't see the road.

qa.q: What could Avni do after some time has passed?
qa.a: Talk to Keerthana about how it hurt, listen to her side, and decide whether to rebuild trust.

qa.q: How might Keerthana feel when Avni looked at her?
qa.a: Keerthana was likely ashamed and guilty, going red and looking away.

grounding: A child who shared her biggest secret with her best friend feels devastated when it is betrayed, early practice in trust.

passage:
"Kamal, why aren't you sitting with Eshaan?" his mother asked at the bus stop.
"He's not my best friend any more."
"What happened?"
"I told him I cry when I watch sad films. Only him. And he told the whole cricket team."
"Oh, Kamal."
"They called me Crybaby all day." Kamal's voice cracked. "He was my best friend. I told him everything."
Across the road, Eshaan stood alone, kicking a stone, glancing over.
"Maybe he feels bad," his mother said gently.
"I don't care." But Kamal kept looking at Eshaan too.

qa.q: Who did Eshaan tell Kamal's secret to?
qa.a: He told the whole cricket team.

qa.q: How was Kamal feeling when his voice cracked?
qa.a: He felt hurt and betrayed, because he had trusted Eshaan with everything.

qa.q: What could Kamal's mother help him do next?
qa.a: Help him name the hurt and, when he's ready, talk with Eshaan about what happened and whether to forgive.

qa.q: How might Eshaan be feeling across the road?
qa.a: Eshaan seems guilty and lonely, standing alone kicking a stone and glancing at Kamal.

grounding: A child shared a secret with his best friend and feels devastated when it is spread, early practice in vulnerability.

passage:
I'm Irawati, and in Class 4 my best friend was Ankita. We did everything together. I told her things I'd never told anyone, like that I was scared my parents would divorce because they fought at night.
One day she was angry with me over a game. At lunch she told the other girls, "Irawati's parents are getting divorced."
I felt like someone had punched my stomach. I ran to the toilet and cried until the bell. I didn't eat.
Ankita came to find me after school. She was crying too. "I didn't mean it. I was just angry."
I didn't talk to her for a week. It was the loneliest week of my life. Then I let her sit with me again, but I didn't tell her secrets for a long time.

qa.q: What did Ankita tell the other girls?
qa.a: She told them, "Irawati's parents are getting divorced."

qa.q: How did Irawati feel when Ankita told the secret?
qa.a: Irawati felt devastated and betrayed, as if punched in the stomach, crying until the bell.

qa.q: What did Irawati do after the betrayal, and was it a wise choice?
qa.a: Irawati stayed away for a week, then let Ankita sit together again but held back secrets; it was a careful way to rebuild trust slowly.

qa.q: How might Ankita have felt when she came to find Irawati?
qa.a: Ankita probably felt guilty and sorry, crying and explaining she had been angry.

grounding: A child who shared a deep worry with a best friend is devastated when the friend tells others, early practice in trust.

passage:
Class 5 note, week before the Christmas break.
Sarika and Sunaina have been inseparable since June: same bench, matching hair clips, notes passed in a code only they understand. Today at the class party, Sunaina told a group that Sarika still sleeps with a stuffed elephant. The group laughed. Sarika went completely white, ran to the washroom, and I found her crying so hard she couldn't speak. She kept saying, 'I only told her. Only her.' I sat with her until she could breathe, then spoke with Sunaina separately. Sunaina said she hadn't meant it to be mean and began to cry too. Next step: on Monday I will offer them quiet time together to talk, with me nearby, and let Sarika decide if she wants that.

qa.q: What did Sunaina tell the group?
qa.a: That Sarika still sleeps with a stuffed elephant.

qa.q: What did Sarika feel when the group laughed?
qa.a: Sarika felt shocked and betrayed, going white and crying because she had trusted only Sunaina with it.

qa.q: Why is letting Sarika decide about Monday's talk a good step?
qa.a: It respects how hurt Sarika is and gives back some control, while still offering a safe chance to repair the friendship.

qa.q: How might Sunaina be feeling after the party?
qa.a: Sunaina seems regretful and upset, crying because she hadn't meant to be cruel to her best friend.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a girl devastated when her one best friend reveals a shared secret at a festive party.

passage:
Dussehra holidays, Friday night.
Dear diary, Pema is my best friend. I've told him everything: that I'm scared of the dark, that I cried when our dog died, that I want to be a chef, not an engineer. He's the only one who knows the chef part. We promised to make the Ravana model together for the colony contest. Today I went to his house with the bamboo sticks, and he and Tsering were already building it. Pema said, 'Tsering's dad has a glue gun, sorry yaar.' Sorry yaar!! Like it's nothing. I walked home and my chest hurt like someone was sitting on it. Now I keep thinking, what if he tells Tsering the chef thing too? I'm never telling anyone anything ever again.
Lokesh

qa.q: What were Pema and Tsering already building?
qa.a: The Ravana model for the colony contest.

qa.q: What does Lokesh's chest hurting 'like someone was sitting on it' show?
qa.a: It shows Lokesh felt crushed and betrayed after Pema broke their promise so casually.

qa.q: What could Lokesh do instead of never telling anyone anything again?
qa.a: Lokesh could tell Pema honestly how much it hurt and ask about the chef secret, giving the friendship a chance to repair.

qa.q: How might Pema see what happened?
qa.a: Pema may think it was a small practical choice because of the glue gun, not realising how deeply it hurt his best friend.

grounding: A child's festival diary records deep hurt when the one best friend who knows every secret breaks a promise.

passage: At Teej the whole village hung swings from the neem trees, and Vasudha and Ishita had planned it for weeks: matching green bangles, one swing, taking turns, just the two of them. They had even linked little fingers and sworn to be best friends forever. But on the day, a new girl from the city, Rhea, arrived with shiny mehendi cones, and Ishita went straight to her. By afternoon the two were on the swing together, laughing, and when Vasudha came up, Ishita said, 'There's no room.' Vasudha stood there in her green bangles until her eyes stung, then walked home alone along the canal. She didn't touch her ghevar. When her mother asked, she only said, 'I'm never having a best friend again.'

qa.q: What did Vasudha and Ishita wear to match?
qa.a: Matching green bangles.

qa.q: How did Vasudha feel standing by the swing?
qa.a: Vasudha felt hurt and betrayed, her eyes stinging, after being told there was no room.

qa.q: How could Vasudha's mother help her that evening?
qa.a: She could listen to what happened and let Vasudha be sad, then gently say that one hurt doesn't mean every friendship ends this way.

qa.q: What might Ishita be feeling on the swing with Rhea?
qa.a: Ishita is probably excited by the new girl and her mehendi, perhaps not thinking about how Vasudha feels.

grounding: At a village festival a girl devoted to one best friend is devastated when that friend leaves her out for someone new.

passage: Snow had piled up to the school fence in Sapporo, and Aiko and Noa built their usual snow lantern in the corner of the yard. Only Noa knew Aiko's secret: she still slept with a worn stuffed rabbit called Mochi. Aiko had whispered it in autumn, under the slide, pinky fingers locked. On Friday, three girls giggled as Aiko walked past. "Say goodnight to Mochi!" one sang. Aiko looked at Noa. Noa stared down at a pair of red mittens. That evening Aiko did not touch her curry. She sat on the stairs holding Mochi and told her mother, "I'm never telling anyone anything again."

qa.q: What was the name of Aiko's stuffed rabbit?
qa.a: Mochi.

qa.q: What was Aiko feeling when she sat on the stairs holding Mochi?
qa.a: She felt betrayed and deeply hurt, because the one person she trusted had let the secret out, so she decided never to tell anyone anything again.

qa.q: How could Aiko's mother support her that evening?
qa.a: She could sit beside Aiko, say how much it hurts to be let down by a best friend, and gently add that sharing with the right person can still be worth it 🤍.

qa.q: Why might Noa have stared at the mittens instead of speaking?
qa.a: Noa probably felt ashamed and caught out, knowing the secret had come from them, and did not know how to face Aiko.

grounding: A child shares a secret with one best friend and is devastated when it is betrayed, a painful first lesson in how risky and precious closeness is.
